name: Dana Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach clarinet at the school, lead a Friday wind group and take recording calls when local groups need a clean part. I have a music master’s, and getting a beginner to breathe without squeezing the reed is still a satisfying hour.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Waiting for the school to decide next year’s teaching hours. A concert can fall through too, but the contract pays the regular bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my wind group that AI can tidy the rehearsal list, but it cannot play the last note together for us. We would keep our Friday practice and the school concerts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have roughly three months of expenses saved, and my teaching contract runs through next summer. I still watch the school budget because a missed renewal would send me looking for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I would keep teaching clarinet and leading the Friday wind group. Before January I would ask the school secretary for the next concert dates and write them into the usual paper diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than frightened. There are a few other music posts nearby, but I would rather keep the pupils I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one cancelled concert mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If one concert is cancelled, the savings cover the gap. I would still call the community hall about a replacement date, because I dislike spending savings for something I can earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you already use AI for any part of a concert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI sometimes to check a programme note, but I still read every line. Parents should hear my wind group play, not admire a tidy description.

say: I would tell the **wind group** that a tidy list does not replace playing together.
I would keep **school concerts** on the calendar.
think: My **three-month cushion** and teaching contract make one cancellation manageable.
A missed **school renewal** would still force me to search for work.
do: Keep **clarinet lessons** and Friday wind rehearsals this term.
Ask the **school secretary** for concert dates before January.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about renewal, while current pay and savings remain sound.
S0.quote: Parents should hear my wind group play, not admire a tidy description.
fieldNote: Her **contract** lasts through next summer, supporting the mild mood despite a renewal worry.
Her occasional **AI use** is a checked programme note, not a new retraining plan.

steps.text: Keep school clarinet lessons and Friday wind rehearsals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the head teacher that AI may write notes, check parts and book halls, so we should protect live lessons in the budget. I would offer to show how pupils sound after a term with a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The little recording commissions I do for local groups could disappear first. If school administrators decide software covers practice, my renewal may also be less certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would give the head teacher a one-page record of pupils who stayed through a full term. In the first year of this change, I would observe a trusted colleague using AI to check instrument ranges, then try it on one piece only after checking the printed parts myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious if my school hours were questioned. My music recordings bring in small fees, but the school teaching contract pays my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for an AI tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy a subscription on a promise. I would try the school’s existing tool only if it is approved and does not send pupil names outside the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you take to the head teacher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The head teacher should see the beginner who can hold a note after three months. A list of software features will not show what my lessons are worth.

say: I would ask the school to protect **live lessons** as booking and checking become automated.
I would show the head teacher **pupil progress** over a term.
think: Local **recording fees** may disappear before school teaching does.
A weaker **contract renewal** would matter far more than the small recordings.
do: Take a **pupil retention record** to the head teacher next month.
Watch a **trusted colleague** use the approved school AI tool only if pupil names stay inside school.
Try **one score** after that demonstration, checking printed parts myself.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible cut to my paid teaching hours.
S1.quote: My music recordings bring in small fees, but the school teaching contract pays my rent.
fieldNote: She uses a **tested school tool** only after approval and checks each score herself.
Her central exposure is **renewal risk**, while recording commissions are a smaller immediate loss.

steps.text: Keep showing the head teacher full-term pupil progress
Watch trusted colleague use approved school AI only if pupil names stay inside school
Try one AI-checked score after the demo and verify printed parts myself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the wind group that AGI by 2028 could draft and teach on a screen, but the school must decide who is responsible for a child in the room. I would ask for a clear contract decision before the new year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recording fees would probably go in 2028, and the school might use AGI to reduce paid lessons. Robots that can do hands-on work follow around 2031, so a live clarinet demonstration has a few more years, but that does not guarantee my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask the school when my contract renewal is decided and list two other schools with open music vacancies. If AGI cuts my lessons in 2028, I would apply for those posts only while vacancies remain and cut the rented recording booth before savings fall below two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious while the contract is intact, alarmed if lessons actually get cut. Three months in the bank gives me some room, not a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What expense would go if recording work stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booth is 75 a month. I would stop renting it only if recording clients disappear; otherwise it pays for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could family help with without replacing pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my mother to watch me practise an audition, not to pay my rent. She taught me to turn up prepared, and I can still do that.

say: I would demand a **contract decision** before the school changes paid lessons.
I would say **in-room teaching** still carries responsibility for children.
think: My **recording fees** likely disappear in 2028, before hands-on robots around 2031.
A school **lesson cut** would threaten rent despite three months saved.
do: Ask the school about **renewal timing** and check two vacancies this week.
Apply to **open school posts** if 2028 AGI cuts my lessons.
Cancel the **75 booth rental** if recording clients disappear, before savings fall below two months.
feel: I feel **anxious** now and would be alarmed if paid lessons fell.
S2.quote: Three months in the bank gives me some room, not a new career.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the **2028 thinking work loss** from the later 2031 robot threat to live performance.
Her **job search** requires real vacancies, and booth cancellation requires lost clients.

steps.text: Apply to open music posts if school lessons shrink after 2028
Cancel 75 booth rental if clients vanish before savings fall below two months
Keep clarinet lessons while the school contract remains active

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the school that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to prove what a beginner learns with a teacher. I would offer to mentor one junior music teacher if the school funds the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would expect recording work to shrink by 2031, but I might save enough to live on the school post. Stage robots around 2034 are a separate question for concerts, and I cannot tell if parents would pay to hear them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I would ask the school to fund two paid mentoring hours a month for a junior teacher. If approved, I would take the apprentice through one beginner class; after 2031 I would keep teaching if the contract renews and check concert fees before accepting dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy if the contract remained secure. Five years would let me build savings and show the school a good class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you mentor without paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not mentor for free after school hours. The junior teacher needs a paid path as much as I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school refuses the mentoring hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the school declines, I would keep my own classes and ask again next budget year. I would not count mentoring pay until it appears on a contract.

say: I would offer **paid mentoring** for a junior teacher if school funds it.
I would show the school **beginner progress** before 2031.
think: My **recording income** may shrink by 2031, while school pay could remain.
I cannot predict what families choose when **2034 stage robots** appear.
do: Request **two paid mentoring hours** monthly from the school this term.
Keep **beginner classes** after 2031 if my contract renews.
Check **concert fees** before accepting dates after 2031.
feel: I feel **uneasy** if the school post remains secure through the longer runway.
S3.quote: The junior teacher needs a paid path as much as I do.
fieldNote: Her proposed junior mentoring plan requires **funded school hours**, never assumed unpaid work after lessons.
She uses the **five-year window** to build savings and prove beginner outcomes.

steps.text: Mentor a junior music teacher if school funds two monthly hours
Keep beginner clarinet classes after 2031 if contract renews
Check concert fees before accepting dates after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my pupils that AGI by 2036 leaves a decade to learn an instrument properly. I would tell the school that a long lead time is a reason to keep teaching, not to freeze hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I could have six months saved if my school contract keeps renewing. Robots around 2039 may change live concerts, but a child learning to listen alongside another child still seems worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put a small part of each school payment into a separate account starting now, but only after bills are covered. In the first year after 2036 I would compare actual school hours and concert fees with the previous year before deciding whether to audition elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy, with a present contract and enough savings for ordinary gaps. I would still read the school budget each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is six months of savings already there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months is a goal, not cash I have already saved. If renewal fails earlier, I would use the current cushion while applying for another school post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a younger player to inherit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope a younger player can learn from me and later take the baton. I do not need a machine to promise that; I need a school to pay the next teacher.

say: I would ask schools to keep **teaching posts** open through the decade.
I would tell pupils that **playing together** is worth learning.
think: I could reach a **six-month cushion** if my contract keeps renewing.
I expect **2039 robots** to test concerts more than school listening.
do: Save a **small part** of school pay after bills from now onward.
Compare **school hours** and concert fees after 2036 before auditioning elsewhere.
Apply for **another school post** if my contract renewal fails before 2036.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about budgets, though my present contract supports ordinary gaps.
S4.quote: Six months is a goal, not cash I have already saved.
fieldNote: She makes the **six-month savings target** conditional on school contracts that continue to renew.
Her long view values **paid succession** for younger teachers, consistent with her apprenticeship outlook.

steps.text: Save part of school pay after bills if contracts keep renewing
Compare school hours and concert fees after 2036
Apply for another school post if contract renewal fails before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recording fees could go before my contract is renewed. A timely school decision, open teaching vacancies and paid mentoring hours would give me something solid to plan around.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the next teacher can afford to learn from the current one. A school cannot call mentoring valuable and leave the hours unpaid.

headlineQuote: A school cannot call mentoring valuable and leave the hours unpaid.
portrait: At **27**, Dana leads wind rehearsals, teaches clarinet and records music with a master’s degree and three months saved.
Her school **contract** pays regular bills; occasional recording fees matter less but may vanish first.
She tries **AI cautiously** on approved material after checking printed parts herself.
She favours **paid apprenticeship** and builds a cushion while school contracts continue to renew.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may erase recording fees before Dana knows whether her school contract renews.
whatWouldHelp: A timely **contract decision**, open vacancies and funded mentoring hours would let Dana plan from paid work.
